intro: Arkansas Legislative Audit examines every county, city, and school district and publishes what it finds. This page quotes what the auditors reported about Clark County's governments, from the reports in our document library — no verdict added in either direction. What the auditors said is the record; what to make of it is yours.
regulatory_basis_note: Read this before reading any Arkansas audit: county and city reports carry a technical 'adverse opinion' on GAAP grounds because Arkansas law has them keep books on a simpler 'regulatory basis.' That phrase appears in every such audit in the state and signals the accounting format — not wrongdoing. A report is 'clean' or not in its findings, deficiencies, and noncompliance sections, which is what this page quotes.

verdicts.detail: No material weaknesses in internal control were identified. Federal grant compliance is audited separately and that report had not yet been issued.

Machine reading of both reports surfaced no findings, deficiency, or noncompliance language beyond standard definitions. These older-format reports are queued for a page-by-page visual pass before we call them clean outright.

rebate.title: The $1.3 million the county owes the state — what it actually is
rebate.body: In July 2026 the county learned it must return about $1.3 million of local sales tax to the state, at $75,000 a month for 18 months. The mechanism is ordinary: Arkansas caps local sales tax on any single large purchase, and businesses may lawfully claim rebates of what they paid past the cap. Businesses claimed those rebates; the state passes the clawback to the county. The county treasurer had anticipated it, and the county judge told the quorum court the receipts had looked inflated. One thing worth knowing: the state does not disclose which businesses claimed the rebates — that anonymity is state practice, not a county choice.
rebate.status: News lead (the Arkadelphian, July 14, 2026) — the DFA notice and repayment schedule are documents worth requesting for the corpus.

limits: Audits test compliance and controls — they do not judge whether spending choices are wise, whether deputy pay should be higher, or whether $1.84M in economic development incentives is well aimed. Those are policy questions, and they belong to residents and elected officials, not auditors.
Clean audits and unposted records can both be true. Nothing here contradicts the gaps on the docket; it means the referee found the books kept by the rules.
The FY2024 county audit is not yet published; this page updates when it is.
minutes_finding: First OCR result from the archived minutes (December 8, 2025 regular session): Ordinance 2025-21 — the 2026 budget this whole site navigates — was adopted unanimously, all eleven justices voting Yea by name. The same meeting adopted the 2026 property tax levy (Ordinance 2025-19) and Ordinance 2025-22, 'amending and adopting a base pay threshold for all new full-time county employees beginning January 1, 2026' — a pay-structure move worth reading in full alongside the deputy-pay question. Obtaining 2025-22's text is now on the docket.
